transcript.content:
Honestly I'd be surprised if the Moon can be seen right now, but give me your honest estimate anyway.

I'm in Davis, California, USA at 2026-09-24 18:42 PDT (UTC-0700) (2026-09-25T01:42:00Z in UTC), at latitude 38.5449 degrees and longitude -121.7405 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 3.014 degrees and its azimuth is 266.753 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 6.78 degrees and its azimuth is 103.997 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 96.97 percent illuminated, 159.91 degrees from the Sun, and 385592.3 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

**Probably yes—but it would be a somewhat challenging, horizon-dependent sighting.**

The Moon is nearly full (**97% illuminated**) and well separated from the Sun (**160°**), so it has excellent intrinsic visibility. It is also on the opposite side of the sky: look **east-southeast**, around azimuth **104°**.

The limiting factor is its very low altitude, only **6.8°**—roughly one fist-width below the horizon when held at arm’s length. At that elevation:

- atmospheric extinction and haze reduce its contrast;
- trees, buildings, or terrain may block it;
- the bright sky shortly before sunset makes initial detection harder.

Because the Sun is only **3° above the western horizon**, twilight is imminent and the eastern sky should already be less bright than the area near the Sun. In a clear sky with an unobstructed ESE horizon, an ordinary observer who knows where to look would have a **fair-to-good chance**, perhaps **around 60–80%**. Binoculars would make it easy, but avoid sweeping anywhere near the Sun.

So my honest estimate: **visible to the unaided eye if your eastern horizon is clear, but not necessarily obvious at first glance.** Waiting several minutes should improve contrast as the Sun sets, though the Moon will also be descending.
